Forget PlayOnLinux, Lutris is the king in the Linux Gaming world now.

There is a lot to cover, so this post will be less of a guide, and more a general overview of the different sections in the Lutris GUI, where it stores files, adding new runners, syncing game libraries etc...

Lutris, Important File Locations

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/runners

Any Runners you have installed will be saved here.

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/runtime

Linux Library Files, as well as any required Windows DLLs, are stored in here. When you use DXVK, for example, any versions you have set to use on your Game Library will be stored in this location.

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/banners

Images used for each game, when set to grid view, are saved in here. You do not need to save images that you want to use for your games in this location, to manually add them yourself, but it is advisable to use this central location, to avoid forgetting where you saved a banner for a specific game.

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/pga.db

This file is your Game Library database, which contains various information about how you have Lutris setup, such as what games you have configured, their current status etc...

/home/{Your_Username}/.config/lutris

Lutris configuration files are stored here.

Lutris.cfg contains the preferences for the Lutris UI.

./runners contains individual configuration files for each of the runners you have installed.

./games as you would image, contains configuration files for each of the games you have installed.

Lutris Interface Overview

Explaining GUI layouts in text format is never fun, so let's get this over with.

The Top Menu

  • Lutris - Basically the main menu. Here you can connect to or register a Lutris.net account, if you do not yet have one (not required to use the software); change your library sync settings (import games) and sync your game library; manage the installed runners - the software that will run games, steam, wine etc...; and change the global preferences.

  • View - Allows you to change the visual style of the program, as well as how it displays your installed games (grid, list etc...).

  • Game - As the name implies, allows you to manage a game you currently have selected, as well as open the Add Game window for adding another game.

  • Help - A pretty much useless menu item, as all it contains is the About page. Though you can see what version of Lutris you are running from here.

Left-Hand Section

Here you can see a list of all the Runners you currently have installed. Right-clicking on any of these entries will provide a context menu for managing that Runner, or else, making it run.

The second list is just a set of filters for refining which games you see in the Library list.

Main Section - Library List/Grid

Your configured/detected games will be listed here. Right-clicking on a game's entry will provide a context menu where you can: run; configure; browse the game's directory on disk; remove; and view the game's entry, if it exists, on the Lutris website.

Common Lutris Tasks

Setting Global Preferences

Clicking on Lutris > Preferences from the main menu, will bring you to the Global Preferences window. Here you can define a common set of global settings which will be applied to all Runners and games configured on your Lutris installation.

This is extremely useful in speeding up the deployment of additional Runners and games.

For example, you can set a Main Game Folder, so that whenever you run a Lutris script to install a new game, it will automatically store them in that location.

You can also define standard resolution settings (including which monitor games should launch on, and what should be done with any additional monitors), set common Environment Variables that you want applied to all games/runners, and apply common fixes to PulseAudio, such as Reducing Latency to fix stuttering or no sound in some games.

These settings, while Global, can be overridden by the same settings being applied to Runners, or individual games in your library.

The order of priority goes from: Global > Runner > Game, so any System Options setting you have applied to a game, will override those specified for the Runner executing the game, and any of the same settings applied in the Global Preferences.

Adding a new Runner

Runners is a term used by the Lutris project to describe third party software which is used to run games. Steam, therefore, is classed as a Runner, as is Wine, and even your Browser, as that can be used to run web-based games.

Lutris stores all runners currently installed in the following folder, with the exception of your currently installed browser:

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/runners

To add a new Runner, you would click on Lutris > Manage Runners or by clicking on the Manage Runners icon from the row beneath the main menu (3 cogs icon).

This will present you with a complete list of all the Runners available which can be added to Lutris. To add one, simply click on Install.

For example, if we clicked on Install for the Atari800 Runner, it would download the required files for that Runner and store them in "/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/runners" and then remove the Install button, once successful.

Configuring a Runner

Each Runner has some specific settings which can be customized; useful, if you want to speed up adding a new game which uses that Runner, by having some common settings already applied and remove the need to type them out for each game you install.

For example, the Atari800 Runner, if you click on the Configure button, has settings for where the BIOS file is located, and which Atari console it should be trying to emulate. These settings would then auto apply to any game you try to add, using the Atari800 runner, though you can override them on a game-by-game basis.

The System Options tab grants you the ability to change further system settings, to be applied only when using that particular Runner. This is useful, if you have a specific Runner which does not play nicely with some of the System Options you set under Global Preferences, or if you just want games for that Runner to be stored somewhere else on disk automatically.

Importing Games/Syncing Games

Not much to this process. Clicking on Import Games from the Lutris menu will open a screen with a set of sliders and Sync buttons to individually Sync games from just those applications.

This process is not perfect, but useful to see how many of your already installed Steam, Wine_Steam and other games can be added to Lutris automatically. Any it fails to find will need to be added manually, which is discussed in the: Lutris, Add and Setup a Game guide.

Managing Wine Versions

This, for me, is one of the major reasons to use Lutris for gaming on Linux using Wine. If you were at all daunted by the previous Guides and the thought of installing Wine via the terminal and manually adding patches etc.. then Lutris has a nice facility to allow you to pick and choose which versions of Wine, including those with additional patches, that you want to use.

Click on Lutris > Manage Runners, and then scroll down the list until you arrive at Wine. Click on the Manage Version button.

Here you can see a list of all the Wine builds that are available for Lutris, and they go back a fair way, from version 1.17.3 -to- 3.13, as of writing this post. The name of the Wine version will denote if that is a standard Wine build, or tailored to work better with a specific game, or contains additional patches, such as Staging, ESync or PBA.

Simply click on the check-box for the Wine version you want and wait a few seconds. This menu is slightly buggy in the current Lutris release, so you won't see anything happen right away, but a few seconds after clicking on the check box, you should see a percentage bar appear and the Wine version you selected will be downloaded to:

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/runners/wine

It will then be available for selection when configuring/installing a game that uses Wine as the Runner.
